title: Karmic tail 3-7-22 in the destiny matrix: the escape that takes the prison with it

seo.title: Karmic tail 3-7-22 in the destiny matrix: the Prisoner and his cell
seo.description: 3-7-22 is the karmic tail called the Prisoner: The Empress, The Chariot and The Fool. Why escape takes the prison along, what Waite and Wen say, and a way out.

short: The karmic tail 3-7-22 is The Empress at the entry, The Chariot as the mechanism and The Fool at the root. It is known as the Prisoner, and its scenario is easy to recognise: a warm home slowly turns into walls, a person breaks out of the walls by force, and in the new place exactly the same walls grow up. Escape does not help, because the prison travels with the escapee. Why this happens can be read in the cards themselves: Waite describes three of the four through one and the same door, a door that is closed to them. The fourth card does not need that door. It leaves by another road.

paragraphs: The legends about the 3-7-22 tail contradict each other, and the contradiction is more interesting than any one of them. The first version: in a past life the soul lost its freedom — prison, captivity, slavery, hospital walls, a body chained to a bed. The second says the exact opposite: the soul itself kept others locked up, controlled the people close to it and broke other people's boundaries. A third adds cells entered by choice: wine, debts, lawsuits. Hence the "program" for this life that popular sites retell: a thirst for freedom together with the fear of losing it, dependence on someone else's will, loans, a difficult bond with the mother. The tail has a second name too — the Inmate.

None of this can be checked. Numbers say nothing about past lives, and the tarot books on which the meanings of the arcana rest know nothing of the matrix or of karmic tails. And yet almost every detail of the legend can be found in the divinatory lists of Arthur Edward Waite, the author of the classic tarot deck and of the book that explains it (1910):

ul: The Chariot reversed: "Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat";
Justice, which stands in the centre of the chart: "Law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity";
The Fool: "Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy…" — the wine and the debts of the legend stand side by side here;
The Tower, which every holder of 3-7-22 has in Manipura, reversed: **"oppression, imprisonment, tyranny"**. The word is right there: imprisonment;
The Empress is linked by Benebell Wen, author of Holistic Tarot (2015), with Saint Adelaide, patron saint of, among others, "abuse victims, prisoners, and exiles".

paragraphs: There are no reversed cards in the matrix: a calculated number does not lie upside down. But a divinatory list is a dictionary of the whole card, and both halves of it belong to the same arcanum. Put these words together and you get something close to a court record of that very legend.

Even the tail's Russian name says more than it seems to. Uznik, "prisoner", comes from uzy, "bonds" or "fetters". The same root gives uzel ("knot"), vyazat ("to tie"), obyazannost ("duty") and **soyuz, "union" — literally "shared bonds"**. Russian uses one word for shackles and for the tie between people who love each other: the bonds of marriage, family bonds, the bonds of friendship. English does much the same with "bonds" and "bondage". For a tail that begins with The Empress — the card of home, family and fruitfulness — this is a perfect fit. Here a person becomes a prisoner not in a cellar, but inside their own union.

sections.h2: The Empress at the entry: a door that only leads in
paragraphs: The Empress is the most generous card in the deck. Waite places her among stars, ripening corn and falling water and calls her "the fruitful mother of thousands" and "universal fecundity". But his other definition matters more: she is "the inferior Garden of Eden, the Earthly Paradise, all that is symbolized by the visible house of man". The Empress is the home. Not the building, but everything it lives on: food, warmth, children, things, shared plans.
Her divinatory list is just as rich: "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". But the same list holds "the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance".

Then Waite writes a sentence worth reading his whole chapter for. The card of The Empress, he says, signifies **"the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life, as into the Garden of Venus; and then the way which leads out therefrom, into that which is beyond, is the secret known to the High Priestess"**. The Empress knows how to get in. She does not know how to get out: that is another card's secret. The High Priestess is not part of the 3-7-22 tail.

This is how the circle begins. A person with this tail enters life — a relationship, a job, a city, a family — through The Empress: generously, physically, with care. They feed, furnish, invest. Everything they touch grows: connections, belongings, duties, people who depend on them. Fruitfulness knows no limit; that is what fruitfulness is. And one day the garden they have grown closes around the gardener like a living hedge. Nobody locked them in. The walls grew out of what they planted themselves.

Wen repeats the theory that The Empress was modelled on Saint Adelaide of Italy, wife of the emperor Otto the Great. For a tail called the Prisoner it would be hard to find a more fitting heroine. In 951 the widowed queen Adelaide was seized by Berengar of Ivrea, who wanted her to marry his son, and held for four months in a fortress on Lake Garda. She escaped, hid in the marshes and waited for her rescuer: Otto came to Italy with an army and married her that same year. Eleven years later she was crowned empress in Rome. A captive freed by a conqueror on the chariot of war, who then became an Empress — two cards of the tail in a single life. No wonder the Church honours her as the patron of prisoners and exiles. In the same chapter Wen gives a second story: the three daughters-in-law of a French king, imprisoned after the Tour de Nesle affair.

sections.h2: The Chariot as the mechanism: a liberator in chains
paragraphs: For Waite, The Chariot is victory. The charioteer **"has led captivity captive; he is conquest on all planes—in the mind, in science, in progress, in certain trials of initiation"**. "Led captivity captive" is not Waite's own phrase but a line from the Psalms, repeated by the apostle Paul: "When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive". The image comes from a triumphal procession: the victor rides into the city, and the captives are led before him. The words have a second reading as well — the victor has taken captivity itself prisoner and set its captives free. The tail needs both. The Chariot leads people into captivity and frees them at the same time.

But Waite spends the whole of his second paragraph on The Chariot on the limits of this victory. Its conquests are outward, not inward. And above all: **"the liberation which he effects may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding"**. A liberator who stays in chains himself — that is the mechanism of 3-7-22.

The same paragraph holds one more detail. If the charioteer "came to the pillars of that Temple between which the High Priestess is seated", Waite writes, "he could not open the scroll called Tora, nor if she questioned him could he answer". The very Priestess who knows the way out of The Empress's garden. The mechanism that is supposed to lead the way out falls silent before the keeper of the exit.
The divinatory list holds the same double edge: "Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble". Help and war on a single line.

Wen notices something easy to miss: the charioteer's armour is "a hard encasing over vulnerable human flesh". The Chariot person, she writes, "likes to appear in control, but has a tendency to run from his or her problems (or attack the problems with such aggression as to subdue it and therefore avoid true, mature confrontation)". And she asks the question on which the whole mechanism of the tail turns: who exactly is in control — the sphinxes that pull the chariot, or the charioteer?

The mechanism of 3-7-22 runs in two modes, and they only look like opposites. The first is escape. When the garden closes in, The Chariot breaks out: a sudden resignation, a move, a break-up, "I can't take it any more", a suitcase packed overnight. The second is control. If there is nowhere to run, The Chariot takes the reins: schedules, rules, checks, "this is how we do things here". A person becomes the warden so as not to feel like the prisoner. Hence the quarrel between the legends — prisoner or jailer. The cards answer: both, by turns and sometimes at once.

In both modes freedom is understood as distance or as power. The best illustration of this mistake is a parable from the sixteenth-century Chinese novel Journey to the West; we will come back to its hero. Sun Wukong, the Monkey King, who has routed the armies of Heaven, makes a wager with the Buddha: if he can leap out of the Buddha's palm, Heaven is his. Wukong somersaults — a single somersault of his covers 108,000 li — and reaches the edge of the world, where five pink pillars stand. On one of them he writes "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven was here", and at its foot, monkey-fashion, he leaves one more mark. He returns in triumph. The Buddha opens his hand: the inscription is on his middle finger. Then he turns his palm over, the fingers become the Mountain of Five Elements, and Wukong lies beneath it for five hundred years. **The Chariot can fly to the edge of the world. It cannot get out of the palm, because distance is not the point.**

sections.h2: The Fool at the root: a card with no cell of its own
paragraphs: The root of the tail is the deep task for whose sake the whole circle turns. Here stands The Fool, and he is unusual even among the arcana. "Traditionally The Fool card is unnumbered," Wen writes; Waite gives it zero, the matrix gives it twenty-two. The Fool's place in the sequence has wandered: some put him at the beginning, others just before the last card, others at the very end. Waite admits that "the real arrangement of the cards has never transpired". The only card without a cell of its own in the row stands at the root of the tail called the Prisoner.

Waite paints The Fool in words like this. **"With light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him"**, a young man pauses at the edge of a precipice and looks not down but at the sky. The drop holds no terror for him. He is "a prince of the other world on his travels through this one", "the spirit in search of experience". And then: "The sun, which shines behind him, knows whence he came, whither he is going, and how he will return by another path after many days."

Trammels with little power, and another path — two details on which the riddle of the tail is solved. The Fool does not break through and does not conquer. He has no need to smash the walls, because they do not hold him. And he does not come back by the road he left on.

The Fool has a shadow too. His divinatory list in Waite is grim: "Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy…". Reversed: "Negligence, absence… carelessness, apathy, nullity, vanity". This is The Fool's freedom taken on credit. Lightness can be had without freedom: with a bottle, a purchase on loan, a reckless leap, a disappearance. And almost every word on this list was once a reason to lock a person up. The Russian idiom "debt pit" (dolgovaya yama) was once no figure of speech but the name of Moscow's debtors' prison; the insane were shut away in what Russians called "yellow houses". The Fool's shadow leads straight into the very cell The Fool himself is free of.

Wen describes in The Fool a "Peter Pan mentality": boastful, careless and possessing "a willful refusal to take responsibility or be mature". She puts it bluntly: The Fool "is about power, but no product". Then she lists The Fool's relatives in world folklore: Robin Hood, Puck, Kitsune the fox, Sun Wukong and Peter Pan. For the Prisoner tail one thing about this list matters: **three of the five are stories of captivity**. Robin Hood is an outlaw. Sun Wukong is the very one who lay beneath a mountain for five hundred years. And Peter Pan once came home to find bars on the window.

So what does The Fool at the root of 3-7-22 mean? The deep task of the tail is freedom, but not the kind The Chariot wins. Not distance, not power, not victory over walls. The Fool's freedom is lightness inside the world: walking without clinging, a rose in one hand and on the shoulder a bundle that, in Wen's description, holds "all his earthly possessions". In Russian that bundle is uzelok, from the same root as uznik, the prisoner. The freest card in the deck carries its own knot as well. Only a small one.

sections.h2: Justice at the centre: a law the wind does not obey
paragraphs: The centre of the chart is the comfort zone, the point a person returns to when tired. Every holder of 3-7-22 has Justice here. This is not chance but arithmetic: a root of 22 gives a centre of 22 + 22 = 44 → 8.

Justice means rules, accounts, contracts, fair play. Waite's divinatory list: "Equity, rightness, probity, executive; triumph of the deserving side in law". Wen stresses that this is "human-created justice, not divine justice", and reads the curtain behind the figure as man-made law, hung there "as if covering or shielding the yellow light of the natural world". She also writes that Justice is about personal adherence "within the confined scope" of one's own life.

For the Prisoner tail this leads to a simple and uncomfortable conclusion: the walls a person with 3-7-22 runs into are most often built from their own rules. "I have to", "that's how it's done", "I promised", "walking away isn't fair". The Empress's home becomes a prison not when a lock appears on the door, but when the centre starts keeping accounts: who put in how much, who owes whom, what leaving would cost. **Justice at the centre is the warden. But she also holds the keys**: rules a person signed up to themselves, they can also revise themselves.

In the chapter on Justice, Waite makes a remark that reads like a commentary on the whole tail. The moral principle "which deals unto every man according to his works", he writes, "differs in its essence" from spiritual justice: that works "like the breathing of the Spirit where it wills", and "we have no canon of criticism or ground of explanation concerning it". This is a clear echo of the Gospel of John: "The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth." And of The Fool, Waite writes that the sun knows "whence he came, whither he is going". The same Gospel verse sounds in his text both at the centre of the tail and at its root. The law and the wind. A centre that keeps accounts, and a root that no account can hold.

There is a second fact shared by everyone with this tail. In Manipura — the chakra of will, status and money — they all have the triple 8-8-16: Justice, Justice, and The Tower in the emotions column. Waite's Tower is "calamity, disgrace, deception, ruin", "a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe", and, following another author, he sees in it "the ruin of the House of Life". The Empress at the entry is the house; The Tower in Manipura is its collapse. A double Justice piles up rules; The Tower blows them apart. This is what a 3-7-22 escape looks like: not gradual but all at once — a slammed door, a burnt bridge and the feeling that there was no other way.

sections.h2: The key is held by the card the tail lacks
paragraphs: Put all this together and a picture emerges that Waite hardly intended, yet which lies in his text. He speaks of three of the four cards through one and the same absent card — The High Priestess. And each time, it is to set her world apart from theirs:

ul: The Empress is the way into the garden, and the way out is "the secret known to the High Priestess";
The Chariot, before the Priestess, "could not open the scroll called Tora, nor if she questioned him could he answer";
Justice sits between pillars like the Priestess, but "the pillars of Justice open into one world and the pillars of the High Priestess into another".

paragraphs: For Waite, the Priestess keeps inner, secret knowledge that is neither taken by force nor worked out by calculation. She is not in the tail. There is an entry, there is force, there is law — but the key to the door out lies with a card that has no place here.

Only The Fool never mentions the Priestess and has no need of her. He does not unlock the door — he "will return by another path". That is the tail's hint. **The way out of the 3-7-22 circle is not where The Chariot looks for it.** It is not broken open, won or earned. It is found when the storming of the walls stops.

sections.h2: Peter Pan: the window, the bars and the dog kennel
paragraphs: Of all The Fool's relatives in Wen's list, the one closest to the 3-7-22 tail is Peter Pan. Not the cartoon Peter but the one in J. M. Barrie's novel Peter and Wendy (1911). The book contains scenes few people remember, and together they play out this tail almost role by role. The quotations are Barrie's own.

It all begins with an escape. "Wendy, I ran away the day I was born," Peter confesses. Because he heard his father and mother "talking about what I was to be when I became a man". Someone drew up a plan for his life, and he answered it by running away.

Then come the bars. "Long ago," Peter says, "I thought like you that my mother would always keep the window open for me, so I stayed away for moons and moons and moons, and then flew back; but the window was barred, for mother had forgotten all about me, and there was another little boy sleeping in my bed." The narrator adds at once: "I am not sure that this was true, but Peter thought it was true." That is exactly how a past-life legend works: it cannot be checked, but people live by it in earnest.

The third scene is the key one. Near the end of the book Peter flies into the Darlings' nursery ahead of Wendy and orders the fairy: "Quick Tink, close the window; bar it!" Let Wendy think her mother has barred her out, and she will come back with him. **The boy once kept out of his home by bars now bars the window against someone else's child.** The prisoner becomes the warden — just as in the quarrel between the 3-7-22 legends. But Mrs Darling sits at the piano with her head bowed and tears in her eyes, and Peter feels "just as if she were inside him, knocking". He unbars the window and flies away.

The same family has a warden of another kind. On the night of the escape Mr Darling chained up Nana, the dog who served as nurse, and so opened the way into the nursery for Peter. When the children have flown, this man with, in Barrie's words, "a noble sense of justice" decides that the blame is all his, crawls into the dog kennel and swears not to come out until the children return: "No, my own one, this is the place for me." Every morning the kennel, with him inside, is carried to a cab and driven to his office, and every evening it is brought back. This is the Justice at the centre in its purest form: first put someone else on a chain, then sentence yourself to the same kennel — and take your cell with you to work.

And Mrs Darling is the Empress of this story. When her husband in the kennel asks her to shut the window because of the draught, she replies: "O George, never ask me to do that. The window must always be left open for them, always, always."

The children come home, and Barrie ends the chapter with a boy outside the window: Peter watching the happy family — "the one joy from which he must be for ever barred". The same word again as in the story of the bars: barred. And when Mrs Darling offers to adopt him too, Peter asks whether she would send him to school, then to an office, and whether he would soon be a man — and draws back: "Keep back, lady, no one is going to catch me and make me a man."

The whole pattern of the tail fits into one nursery. The window, open or barred, is The Empress. Peter the warrior, the captain, the conqueror of Hook who carries the children off to his island, is The Chariot. Mr Darling in the kennel is Justice handing down its own sentence. The eternal boy who cannot be caught is The Fool seen from his shadow side. And Barrie draws a conclusion without any matrix at all: **the one who most fears being caught stays outside the window for ever**. A freedom guarded against everyone is also a cell — only one without walls.

sections.h2: How the 3-7-22 circle plays out in life
paragraphs: What follows is our reading of the pattern, not a prediction. The cards do not tell what will happen to a particular person; they describe the course along which a person may be carried if nothing is noticed.

paragraphs.h3: In a couple: "holds on tight" and "could vanish at any moment"

paragraphs: For 3-7-22, relationships begin with The Empress, and this is not a figure of speech but a calculation: the relationship line of every holder of this tail opens with a 3. The entry is generous — care, food, a shared household set up fast, keys to the flat within a month. The warmth is real.

Then the garden grows: shared plans, money, friends, routine. One day the person with this tail notices that there is no corner of their life left that does not need accounting for — even if nobody asks for an account. The Chariot switches on. Either escape: coldness, business trips, "I need space", and sometimes a break-up in a single day, prepared in secret. Or control: where are you, who with, why so late. It is easier to become the warden than to admit to feeling like the prisoner.
From the outside such a person looks contradictory: "holds on very tight" and "could vanish at any moment". Both are true. These are the two modes of the same Chariot.

paragraphs.h3: In the family: the window that is shut for the night

paragraphs: In childhood the circle often begins in a home with much love and many rules: the child is fed, taken to clubs — and accounted for every minute. The child learns an equation: being loved means being held. Teenage rebellion in such a child looks like a siege. The Chariot breaks free from care not through talk but through war.

Grown up, a person with 3-7-22 builds a home of their own — and risks repeating the equation from the other side. Either they hold their children the way they were held. Or they are so afraid of becoming a jailer that they vanish themselves: work, travel, an absence that calls itself freedom. "Absence", by the way, is a word from Waite's reversed Fool. The relationship with the mother that the legends talk about belongs here too: the mother is the first Empress in anyone's life, and the accounts may begin with her — for care that was a cage, or for a cage that was called care.

paragraphs.h3: In work and money: freedom on credit

paragraphs: A familiar story: a person leaves a salaried job "so as not to depend on anyone", starts their own business — and two years later works without days off for their own company, their staff and the bank. The Chariot has defeated the boss and taken the charioteer prisoner. Waite was not writing about business, but "the liberation which he effects may leave himself in the bondage" could hardly be put better.

The second story is money as escape. A holiday, a car, a move, a purchase after which "at last I can breathe" — on credit. Extravagance stands in The Fool's list next to intoxication, and they work alike: lightness for an evening, payments for a year. Hence the debts and loans in popular descriptions of the tail. Not because numbers predict debt, but because in this scenario the cheapest door out leads into the next cell.

paragraphs.h3: Inside: two people in one cell

paragraphs: Two people live in the inner world of 3-7-22. One keeps accounts: what is owed, what was promised, what will happen if everything is dropped — this is the Justice at the centre. The other stands at the window and knows that real life is somewhere out there, beyond the glass — this is The Fool at the root. The Chariot rushes between them.

The pressure builds quietly: rules, obligations, "I'll put up with it". Then The Tower in Manipura does its work all at once and with a crash: "that's it, enough". The bridge is burnt, the door has slammed, the person is free. A week later Justice arrives with the question "was that fair?" — and a new rule is added to the old ones: "never do that again". The cell is rebuilt, this time taking the last mistake into account. **The strongest prison in this tail is built from the lessons drawn after the escape.**

sections.h2: The price: what the tail takes if it goes unnoticed
paragraphs: The first price is a life lived in draft. Real life always begins "after": after the divorce, after quitting, after the move, after the children grow up. Until then there is a sentence to serve. Years spent waiting do not come back.

The second is burnt gardens. An escape in Tower style destroys not only the walls but everything that grew behind them. The Empress's garden was never the prison — the prison was the way of living in it. But in the heat of the moment everything goes: relationships, work, friendships, a home that could have been rebuilt rather than blown up.

The third is the convoy. The Chariot "led captivity captive": when it leaves, it takes its captives along. Around a person caught in this circle, others are cast in roles too — wardens to escape from, or prisoners to hold on to. A partner, a child, an employee live by the timetable of someone else's escape.

The fourth is false exits. Intoxication, extravagance, mania — words from The Fool's list. Lightness bought with a bottle, a purchase or a risk is the shortest road into the narrowest cell: addiction, debt, consequences that can no longer be negotiated.

The fifth is the harvest never gathered. The Empress is fruitful, but fruit ripens slowly, and The Chariot is off before the harvest is in. Much begun, little gathered — that very "power, but no product" — and a feeling that life keeps starting over.

If a "false exit" has become an addiction, if debts are out of control, if someone at home holds a person by force, threatens them or will not let them leave — this is no longer a matter for a matrix reading. It needs real people: a psychologist, an addiction specialist, a crisis centre, a lawyer; in danger, call your local emergency number or a local crisis line. A reading of the tail is a language for watching oneself, not a substitute for help.

sections.h2: How to get out without staging an escape: nine practices
paragraphs: The tail cannot be cancelled — it is the arithmetic of a date. And there is no "bad card" in it: home, strength and freedom are all resources in themselves. The task is to change their roles. Let The Empress build a home with doors, let The Chariot carry rather than storm, and let The Fool set the direction.

ol: **Draw a plan of the cell.** Write down everything that feels like walls right now. Next to each, note who put it there: circumstances, other people, or one's own rule. Often half the bars turn out to carry the prisoner's own signature.

**Build the door before the walls.** On entering any new "house" — a job, a union, a project, a loan — agree on the way out in advance: terms, conditions, how people leave here fairly. The Empress is a door, and a door works both ways.

**Small departures instead of great escapes.** Regular, lawful freedom: an evening alone, a walk with no destination, a day trip, a pastime with no result. The Fool walks; he does not break through. Freedom taken a little at a time never has to be taken by storm.

**A pause before The Tower.** When "that's it, enough" hits, allow three days with no irreversible steps: no quitting, no breaking up, no selling. A right decision will still be right on the fourth day — it can just be made without a fire.

**Release the convoy.** Check whom one is holding: the "where are you" calls, decisions made for someone else, care that makes leaving impossible. Each week give someone close a little more freedom than feels comfortable. The warden is freed together with the prisoners.

**Ask "where to", not only "where from".** Before leaving, name not what one wants to get away from, but what one wants to reach. Wen writes that The Chariot travels "not for the sake of travel, but for the sake of acquisition"; Waite's Fool is "the spirit in search of experience". If the only answer is "as far from here as possible", it is an escape, not a journey.
**Name one's own false exits.** Write them down: the bottle, the purchase, the screen, the risk, the vanishing act. And treat them as doors that lead not outside but into the next cell.
**Wait for the harvest.** Bring at least one thing to fruit before starting the next. The Empress needs time, and a gardener who does not leave before autumn.

**Review the rulebook.** Every few months reread one's own "I have to"s and strike out those one would no longer sign today. Justice at the centre is the warden, but she is also the one who signs the release order.

paragraphs: The sign that the circle has loosened is simple: **leaving is possible — and so there is no need to run**. The door is not locked, and a person stays in the house not because they are held, but because they want to.

sections.h2: The strong version of 3-7-22: a house with an open window
paragraphs: The strong version of the tail is not Peter Pan but Mrs Darling: a person who builds houses with open windows. Their Empress is generous without keeping count: a family, a team, a workshop, a business that people come into and are free to leave. Their Chariot is a cart, not a battering ram: they move house, travel, push projects and people forward, but they go where they have decided to go, not wherever the walls happen to end. Their Justice writes fair contracts — with an exit clause. And The Fool at the root gives them what cannot be bought: the ability to be free without leaving.

Such a person is good at freeing others. "Led captivity captive", in its best reading, is about them: they lead people out of dead ends, untangle, help others leave what holds them. Work that leads people out suits them: human rights and law, crisis support, mentoring that lets students go, a business people can leave without bitterness, the open road. In The Empress's reversed list, Waite gives a formula fit to be their motto: **"Light, truth, the unravelling of involved matters"**. A prisoner who has learned to untie knots — the best possible ending for a tail with such a name.

Journey to the West has an ending like that too. Freed from under the mountain, Sun Wukong sets out with the monk Xuanzang to fetch the holy scriptures from the West. Early on the road he puts on a golden headband himself, and from then on every spell his master recites squeezes his head. The headband stays on until the end of the novel. In the last chapter Wukong, now a Buddha, asks for it to be taken off at last — and is told there is nothing to remove: since he has become a Buddha, the band has vanished of itself. Wukong touches his head. The band is gone.
The strong version of 3-7-22 works the same way. A restriction is not torn off or gnawed through. **It vanishes when there is nothing left to hold.**

sections.h2: How to check for the 3-7-22 tail by date of birth
paragraphs: The 3-7-22 tail appears exactly when the three numbers of the date of birth add up to 22. Here is how to count:

ol: A is the day of birth. If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 29 → 11, 30 → 3.
B is the number of the month.
C is the sum of the digits of the year; if it is greater than 22, add the digits again: 1987 → 25 → 7.
If A + B + C = 22, the tail is 3-7-22.

paragraphs: Example: 29.04.1987. A = 11, B = 4, C = 7, total 22. The rest follows by itself:

A root of 22 is never produced by reduction: the three numbers of the date must add up to exactly 22 — hit the ceiling of the scale without spilling over it. The whole tail, centre included, grows out of this one number: 22 + 22 = 44 → 8, 22 + 8 = 30 → 3, 22 + 3 = 25 → 7. And this is the only one of the 26 possible tails with The Fool at the root.
This arithmetic gives facts that hold for every holder of 3-7-22:

ul: the centre of the chart is always Justice, and Manipura is always 8-8-16;
the relationship line always begins with The Empress, and in Svadhisthana the energy column is always The Empress;
in Muladhara the energy column is always The Fool;

people born on the 20th, 21st or 22nd never have this tail; being born with it on the 17th, 18th or 19th is possible only in the twenty-first century, and there are just ten such dates in all of history — the first is 19 January 2000;
people born in 1929, 1938–1939, 1947–1948, 1956–1957, 1965–1966, 1974–1975, 1983–1984 and 1992–1993 never have it: the year number there is 21 or 22, which leaves no room for the day and month;
from 1994 onwards the tail is possible in every year.

paragraphs: How many such people are there? We went through every date from 1 January 1900 to 5 October 2026 — 46,299 days. 1,353 of them give the 3-7-22 tail, 2.92%: thirteenth place out of 26 possible tails. But generations differ. Among people born in 1960–1999 it is 2.72% and the same thirteenth place; among those born in 2000–2025 it is 5.19%, sixth place: almost one in nineteen.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: The calculation follows the classic destiny matrix scheme: the tail is written as M–N–D, where D = A + B + C, the centre E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M, and sums above 22 are reduced by adding their digits. The frequencies come from running every date through the site's calculator.
Arthur Edward Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; 1922 reprint): card symbolism — Part II, divinatory meanings — Part III, history of the designs — Part I. Quoted in the original.
Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015), chapter 9: The Fool, The Empress, The Chariot, Justice, The Tower. Quoted in the original.
J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), chapters 3, 11, 16 and 17; quoted in the original.
Wu Cheng'en, Journey to the West (16th century), chapters 4–7, 14 and 100.
Psalm 68:18 and Ephesians 4:8 ("led captivity captive"), John 3:8 — in the King James Version.
Adelaide of Italy — from standard biographies; the origin of the Russian words uzy, uznik and soyuz — from the etymological dictionaries of Max Vasmer and Nikolai Shansky.

The legends of the tail are a summary of popular destiny matrix descriptions. The link between the three positions, the comparisons with Peter Pan and Journey to the West, the scenes and the practices are the author's interpretation. Waite and Wen do not describe the destiny matrix or karmic tails.

paragraphs: For a couple, 3-7-22 brings the wish to build a good shared life together with the task of preserving freedom and responsibility within it. The Empress at M concerns what you want to grow together; the Chariot at N develops the task through the pace of decisions and progress towards a goal; the Fool at D raises questions of trust, personal space and keeping commitments. This is our reading of Lisovskaya’s pair positions; her book contains no ready-made interpretation of this triple.

The partners might launch a shared project and quickly divide the first jobs. Starting is exciting, but soon one wants to change direction while the other is already counting on the promised result. The Chariot can help complete the next stage; if it merely sets the pace, initial agreement becomes a demand to keep running alongside forever. The Fool in the central task invites a discussion of what freedom each person retains and what they must finish or hand over responsibly.

Before a new undertaking, agree on more than the result: include a trial period, spending limits and a way to leave the project. The difficulty is treating these questions as mistrust, or demanding complete control to protect shared comfort. Freedom becomes practical here when participation can be honestly revised without leaving a partner alone with unfinished work. Shared growth then need not require an indefinite surrender of personal choice.

faq.q: Does the 3-7-22 tail mean prison or trouble with the law?
faq.a: No. The cards do not predict events, and "the Prisoner" is an image of a scenario, not a sentence. About 3% of all birth dates give this tail, and more than 5% among people born after 2000; the lives of the vast majority of these people have nothing to do with prison. Justice at the centre speaks first of all about the rules a person lives by — and with which they can lock themselves in.

faq.q: Who was a person with 3-7-22 in a past life — a prisoner or a jailer?
faq.a: It cannot be checked: numbers say nothing about past lives. But the disagreement between the legends is more accurate than either of them. Waite's Chariot "has led captivity captive" — it both leads captives away and stays in chains itself. In this life a person with this tail can be both: running from control and starting to control others so as not to feel caught.

faq.q: Are the 3-7-22 tail and the "22-7-3 program" the same thing?
faq.a: Yes. They are the same three points M, N and D, written in reverse order, from the root to the entry. Some authors read the tail from the bottom up and write 22-7-3. The cards, their roles and the scenario stay the same.

faq.q: Why is the 3-7-22 tail almost twice as common among children as among their parents?
faq.a: Because of the arithmetic of the year. The tail needs the day, the month and the year number to add up to exactly 22. For the years 1960–1999 the year number is large — from 5 to 22 — and often leaves no room for the day and month. For 2000–2025 it is small — from 2 to 12. So among people born in 1960–1999 the tail occurs in 2.72%, and in 2000–2025 in 5.19%.

faq.q: Why does everyone with the 3-7-22 tail have The Tower in Manipura?
faq.a: Arithmetic again: everyone's centre is 8, and Manipura is calculated from the centre twice, 8 + 8 = 16. The Tower in the emotions column does not promise disasters. It describes how the tension of the will builds up and discharges: enduring for a long time by the rules, then bringing everything down at once. Anyone who knows this habit in themselves can release the tension bit by bit, without waiting for the explosion.

Both tails begin with The Empress, and both contain The Fool, but in different roles. In 3-22-19 The Fool is the mechanism: lightness, carelessness and leaving are how the circle turns, while the root is The Sun and the centre is Strength. In 3-7-22 The Fool is at the root: freedom is the goal itself, and the mechanism is The Chariot, trying to win that freedom by force. The first tail is about escaping into lightness; the second is about ceasing to take freedom by storm.

faq.q: Is the 3-7-22 tail linked to alcohol and addiction?
faq.a: The tail does not predetermine them. "Intoxication" is on Waite's divinatory list for The Fool, and the 3-7-22 legends often mention wine, but a divinatory list says nothing about a particular person. The scenario explains something else: why lightness without freedom can look like a way out. If drinking, gambling or spending has become a way to let off steam, that is a reason to see an addiction specialist or a psychologist, not to look for the answer in the matrix.

No: it is the arithmetic of the date of birth, and that does not change. But the scenario can stop running on its own. The sign is simple — the escapes stop and the doors remain: a person lives in a house they are free to leave, and so does not strain to get out.

faq.q: What if a child has the 3-7-22 tail?
faq.a: Among children born after 2000, almost one in nineteen has it. The main thing is not to teach the child the equation "being loved means being held". Give small freedoms suited to the child's age in advance, so that big ones never have to be taken by storm; explain the rules and agree on them together; do not answer rebellion by tightening the regime. Mrs Darling kept the window open — and the children came back.

faq.q: Is the 3-7-22 tail different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex does not change a single number or a single role. The Empress is not a "women's" card but the card of home, care and fruitfulness: a home is built both by the one who pays for it and by the one who makes it liveable. Only the scenery differs; the scenario is the same.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice here, when tarot books make 8 Strength?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille order of the cards: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. In his 1910 deck Waite swapped these two cards, so in his book Justice is number XI. A card's meaning does not depend on its number: at the centre of the 3-7-22 tail stands Justice — the scales, the sword and the law.

intro: The cards are numbered as in the destiny matrix and the Marseille deck: 8 is Justice, 22 is The Fool. In Waite's deck Justice is number XI and The Fool is zero. The meaning rests on the card's name, not on its number.
report: The legends about the 3-7-22 tail cannot agree on who its holder was in a past life. Some say a prisoner: jail, captivity, hospital walls, wine, debts. Others say a jailer, someone who kept the people close to them locked up and broke other people's boundaries. None of it can be checked: numbers are silent about past lives. But the cards themselves settle the dispute, and their answer is unexpected — both at once.

Even the tail's Russian name points the way. Uznik, "prisoner", comes from uzy, "bonds" or "fetters". The same root gives uzel ("knot"), obyazannost ("duty") and soyuz, "union" — literally "shared bonds". One word covers both shackles and the tie between people who love each other. The tail begins with The Empress, the card of home and family, and here a person becomes a prisoner not in a cellar, but inside their own union.

For Arthur Edward Waite, author of the classic tarot deck, The Empress is "all that is symbolized by the visible house of man": food, warmth, children, shared plans. A person with this tail enters life generously, and everything around them grows: connections, belongings, duties, people who depend on them. And one day the garden they have grown closes around the gardener. Nobody locked them in. The walls grew out of what they planted themselves.

That is when The Chariot switches on. Waite writes that its charioteer **"has led captivity captive"**. The words come from the Psalms, the image of a triumph in which captives are led before the victor. And at once he adds a caveat: "the liberation which he effects may leave himself in the bondage". The Chariot runs in two modes. Escape: walking out in a single day, a suitcase packed overnight. Or control: schedules, checks, "this is how we do things here". It is easier to become the warden than to admit to being the prisoner. That is why the legends quarrel: in this tail a person can be both, by turns or at once.

report.h3: The key lies with a card the tail does not have

report: Waite has a sentence worth reading his whole chapter on The Empress for. Her card is "the door or gate by which an entrance is obtained into this life", and the way out is **"the secret known to the High Priestess"**. The Empress knows how to get in. She does not know how to get out.

The Priestess turns up in Waite twice more, and again next to the cards of this tail. Before her, the charioteer of The Chariot "could not open the scroll called Tora, nor if she questioned him could he answer". And of Justice, which everyone with this tail has at the centre of the chart, Waite says: "the pillars of Justice open into one world and the pillars of the High Priestess into another". Three cards out of four are shut off from one and the same door. And the Priestess herself, the keeper of the exit, is not in the tail.

Only The Fool at the root has no need of her. In Waite's words he walks "with light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him", and one day he "will return by another path". The Fool does not break down walls — they simply do not hold him. The Chariot, meanwhile, looks for the way out through force and distance. In the Chinese novel Journey to the West the Monkey King flies to the edge of the world, writes "The Great Sage Equal to Heaven was here" on a pillar — and learns that it was the Buddha's finger. There is no leaping out of the palm: distance is not the point.

report.h3: The boy who barred the window

report: Benebell Wen, author of Holistic Tarot, names Peter Pan among The Fool's relatives. J. M. Barrie's book has scenes that play out this tail almost role by role. Peter tells how he once came home to find the window barred and another little boy sleeping in his bed. And at the end he flies into someone else's nursery himself and orders the fairy: "Quick Tink, close the window; bar it!" — so that Wendy will think her mother no longer waits for her. **The prisoner becomes the warden.**

Wendy's father, a man with "a noble sense of justice", blames himself for the children's flight, crawls into the dog kennel and swears not to come out until they return. Every morning the kennel, with him inside, is driven by cab to his office. A cell imposed on oneself gets taken along to work. And the mother answers her husband when he asks her to shut the window: "The window must always be left open for them, always, always."

Two people live inside a person with 3-7-22. One keeps accounts: what is owed, what was promised, what will happen if everything is dropped. The other stands at the window and knows that real life is somewhere out there. The pressure builds quietly and comes out all at once: "that's it, enough", the bridge burnt, the door slammed. A week later comes the question "was that fair?" — and a new rule joins the old ones. **The strongest prison in this tail is built from the lessons drawn after the escape.**

The price of the circle is a life lived in draft, where the real thing always starts "after": after the divorce, after quitting, after the move. Burnt gardens that could have been rebuilt rather than blown up. And false exits. Waite's divinatory list for The Fool includes "extravagance" and "intoxication": lightness for an evening, payments for a year. If such an exit has become an addiction, if someone at home holds a person by force or threatens them, real people are needed — a psychologist, an addiction specialist, a crisis centre, and in danger a local emergency number or crisis line.

report.h3: Leaving is possible — so there is no need to run

report: The way out of this circle is not broken open or earned. It is prepared in advance and little by little:

ul: on entering a new job, union or loan, agree at once on how people leave here fairly;
small lawful freedoms instead of great escapes: an evening alone, a day trip;
when "that's it, enough" hits, three days with no irreversible steps;
ask not "where to run from" but "where to go";
every few months, reread one's own "I have to"s and strike out the ones no longer worth signing.

report: The strong version of the tail is not Peter Pan but Mrs Darling: a person who builds houses with open windows. They create a place where things grow and hold no one in it, and they find their motto in Waite's reversed list for The Empress: "Light, truth, the unravelling of involved matters". A prisoner who has learned to untie knots.

In Journey to the West the Monkey King wears a golden headband the whole way, and it squeezes his head. In the last chapter, having become a Buddha, he asks for it to be taken off — and is told there is nothing to remove: the band has vanished of itself. **A restriction is not torn off. It vanishes when there is nothing left to hold.**
